1:
The crowded school is read as a good sign. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes the college to be the one at Gilgal, and supposes that wherever Elisha resided as many as could flocked to him; their wanting room is a good hearing, a sign many are added to them, and his miracles doubtless drew them in. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) corrects the rendering: it is rather the place where we sit before thee, habitually, for instruction, so the common hall is meant. He adds that these disciples did not live in one building like a community of monks, their settlement being called dwellings in the plural, and that they could be married.

Their poverty and industry are drawn from the request itself. Henry notes that when they wanted room they did not speak of cedars and marble and curious artificers, but only of getting every man a beam; that they were poor men with no interest in great ones, too poor to hire workmen or buy tools but obliged to borrow, poverty being no bar to prophecy; and that they were industrious, unwilling to live like idle drones upon the labours of others. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) gathers the same lesson, that although the sons of the prophets principally devoted themselves to religious exercises, they sometimes employed themselves about manual arts. Ellicott supplies the setting, that the Jordan valley was well wooded, its bed still overarched by oleanders, acacias and thorns, so that if all took part the work would soon be done. John Gill (reformed) adds that the place lay some six miles from Gilgal.

The lament over the axe is weighed word by word. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) deny the word means borrowed at all, holding it means begged, and note that the exclamation implied a petition for help. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) keeps the received sense and offers two ways of taking the clause, that it has fallen in and been sought in vain, or that it was borrowed and the loss the more afflicting, adding from Jarchi the words I have nothing wherewith to repay it. Henry builds the man’s character on it: he did not say it was a mischance and who could help it, but cried out with deep concern, for had the axe been his own it would only have grieved him that he could be no further serviceable to his brethren, whereas now it grieved him that he could not be just to the owner. To those who have an honest mind, he adds, the sorest grievance of poverty is being rendered unable to pay their just debts.

What the stick did is the question pressed hardest. Clarke insists it had no natural tendency to raise the iron and was only a sign the prophet chose to use, the floating being a real miracle, since the gravity of the metal must for ever have kept it at the bottom. Ellicott is more exact: the axe-head did not swim but simply rose to the surface, having fallen in near the bank, and the stick was a symbolical act meant to help the witnesses see that the rising was supernatural and wrought through the prophet, as the salt thrown into the spring at Jericho had been; it showed that iron could be made to float like wood by the sovereign power of Jehovah. Keil and Delitzsch dismiss the natural reading repeated by Thenius, that Elisha struck the eye of the axe with a long stick and so levered it up, as needing no refutation, since raising an iron axe that way and making it float is impossible. Henry warns against doubling the miracle the other way, since we need not suppose the stick sank to fetch up the iron: it was enough as a signal of the divine summons to the iron to rise.
8:
The war itself is left unexplained, and the voices say why. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) admits the real or pretended cause cannot be told, and borrows Calmet’s maxim that an ambitious and restless prince always finds a sufficiency of reasons to colour his enterprises; he supposes the Syrian had observed from the disposition of the Israelite army which way it was about to move, and laid his ambuscades accordingly. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) corrects the tense, since the king of Syria was warring continually rather than opening a war, and argues the reign intended cannot be a later one, since here the Syrians achieve nothing. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets the episode beside the last: Elisha serves the king with his spirit of prophecy as he had served the sons of the prophets, since whatever abilities a man has of doing good make him a debtor to the wise and the unwise alike.

The plan the Syrians laid is grammatically obscure, and the two critics divide. Ellicott notes that the phrase for the place means a certain one, I will not mention which, and that the word for my camp occurs only here, its form anomalous and probably corrupt; the Targum renders house of my camp, while the Syriac and Vulgate make it an ambush, which has suggested that the true reading is hide ye, though he thinks it a more obvious change to read ye shall go down. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) defend the received text, holding the word for encamping quite appropriate, so that there is no need either for the alteration into ye shall hide yourselves or for Ewald’s ye shall place an ambush with its arbitrarily postulated meaning. At the next verse Ellicott defends the Authorised Version against those same versions: they deduced hiding from going down, as though crouching on the ground were meant, whereas the word is really an irregular participial form from the verb to descend.

What the king of Israel did with the warning is read three ways. Clarke reports that the Vulgate gives the verse a different turn, that the king sent beforehand and took possession of the place, so that the Syrians were disappointed; this he thinks very likely, though it is not expressed in the Hebrew. Ellicott agrees that he sent a sufficient force to hold the place, so that the Syrians had to return unsuccessful, and reads the words not once nor twice as covering the whole verse, since on more than one occasion and for different inroads Elisha gave forewarning. John Gill (reformed) alone makes it distrust: the king sent spies to see whether the Syrians were there and whether the man of God had told him truth, for he had no hearty respect for the prophet though the prophet had been so serviceable to him. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) says simply that he sent soldiers to secure the place and passage designed.

The alarm at the Syrian court is caught in one word. Ellicott renders it literally storm-tost, a phrase found nowhere else in the Old Testament, and Gill expands the figure: there was as it were a storm in the king’s breast, and he was like a troubled sea, fretting at the disappointment time after time. Of the question he then put, Ellicott reports that the phrase occurs only here, that pointed differently it would yield the Greek sense, who betrays me to the king of Israel, and that Boettcher’s correction, who leads us astray, is better still, being the natural supposition of a king unexpectedly confronting an armed Israelite force. Henry draws the conclusion: a confession of the boundless knowledge of Israel’s God, as before of his boundless power, is here extorted from Syrians, since nothing done or said or thought by any person in any place is out of the reach of his cognizance.
13:
The size of the force sent against one man is thought absurd. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) supposes the king had heard how a captain and his fifty were baffled in the attempt on Elijah, and so sent an army, as if the fire from heaven that consumed fifty could not as easily consume fifty thousand. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) sets the scene: Dothan lay on a hill twelve Roman miles from Samaria, in a narrow pass on the caravan route to Egypt, and the great host was infantry, not an army but a company, come by night to take the town by surprise.

The servant and his opened eyes are handled with care. Ellicott observes that this was one waiting on the man of God, not Gehazi, who is never called Elisha’s minister, and that he had gone out to where the house commanded a view of the valley in which the Syrians lay. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) turns the vision into a question: where is heaven, is it not above, beneath and around us, and were our eyes open as the servant’s we should see the heavenly host in all directions; the horses and chariots of fire were there before ever his eyes were opened.

What was done to the Syrians was not blindness, and three voices say so independently. Ellicott notes that the word is the one used of the blinding at the door in Genesis and nowhere else, denoting not so much blindness as a dazing with mental bewilderment, so that they saw but knew not what. Clarke glosses it as confounding their sight so that they might not know what they saw and might mistake one place for another. Henry is the most precise: not stone-blind, nor so as to be aware of it, for they could see the light, but their sight was so altered that they could not know the persons and places they had been acquainted with before.

Whether the prophet then lied is the chapter’s sharpest question. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) say plainly that his words contain a falsehood, to be judged as every ruse is by which an enemy is deceived. Thenius, as Ellicott reports him, denies any untruth strictly taken, since Elisha’s home was not at Dothan but at Samaria, and the phrase about the man might mean to his house. Ellicott finds it easier to suppose the dazing had set them wandering in the valley, vainly seeking the way up to the city gate, so that a prophet finding them so spoke the literal truth. John Gill (reformed) says he answered most truly, though ambiguously, since he had come out of the city and was going to Samaria; and Henry agrees that he did not lie, for if they would see him they must go to another city.

The clemency is praised, and its effect disputed. Keil and Delitzsch hold that Elisha forbade the killing because the king had not taken them prisoners in war, and because the object of the miracle, to show the Syrians whose prophet they dealt with, would have been frustrated by their deaths. Clarke calls the eagerness to smite them dastardly, since men who in open battle lay down their arms are entitled to their lives, much more those whom providence has put into one’s hand. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) adds policy to piety, that the act was one of singular charity and of no less prudence, since the hearts of the Syrians might thereby be mollified toward Israel. Henry agrees that the most glorious victory over an enemy is to turn him into a friend. Ellicott alone will allow no gratitude: the stress lies on the word bands, for the Syrians, dreading Elisha, gave up clandestine raiding only to try regular war with their whole strength.
24:
The siege prices are quoted as evidence, and the voices price them. John Gill (reformed) notes that Ben-hadad was not at all softened by the humane treatment his forces had met with, and finding he could do nothing by ambush mustered his whole host for open war. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reckons the eighty shekels at about ten pounds, observes that ass’s flesh would not ordinarily be eaten at all and the head is the cheapest part, and brings two parallels: Plutarch, that in a famine among the Cadusians an ass’s head could hardly be got for sixty drachms, and Pliny, that when Hannibal besieged Casalinum a mouse sold for two hundred denarii. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) holds the second item to be no dung at all, the word being of doubtful signification and nowhere else used, but probably a sort of pease which in Arabic bears that name, a coarse food much used among the poorer Israelites.

The king’s reply to the starving woman is read five ways. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reports that some take it as an imprecation, may God save thee not. Gill notes the same marginal rendering, and adds that Josephus understood it so, that being wroth the king cursed her in the name of God. Ellicott holds the received text right, allowing that the margin would be possible in another context, and reads the words as the irony of despair, reminding the woman of what she well knew, that corn and wine were long since exhausted. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) weighs the tone rather than the grammar: some think it a quarrelling word and the language of his fretfulness, but it rather seems to be a quieting word, since till God help us I cannot help thee.

The horror that follows is handled with restraint. Clarke pleads for the mothers so far as he can, allowing that the children may have died of hunger and only then become food for their desperate parents, and reports Jarchi’s view that the hidden child was already dead, hidden so that one mother might eat him alone; Ellicott suggests instead that she hid him to save him. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) observe that the curses of the law had here been literally fulfilled, which made the king rend his clothes. Ellicott explains the garment beneath them: sackcloth was the known garb of penitence, which Jehoram had secretly assumed to appease the wrath of Jehovah, and that a king should wear it was a portent in his subjects’ eyes. Henry grants the grief and denies the repentance: he lamented the calamity but not his own iniquity, nor that of his people, which was the procuring cause of it, so that the foolishness of man perverted his way and then his heart fretted against the Lord.

The oath against the prophet is explained by what Elisha had counselled. Ellicott supposes he had urged unyielding resistance in the steadfast faith that Jehovah would help his own, and had yet brought no help in this hour of need. Clarke leaves it open whether the king attributed the calamities to the prophet or thought he could remove them and would not. Henry marks what the oath replaced: instead of vowing to pull down the calves at Dan and Beth-el, he swore the death of Elisha, as under the persecuting emperors the fault was laid on the Christians whenever the empire groaned. Keil and Delitzsch note that the elders were gathered in the prophet’s house, probably for counsel and consolation, which shows what position he held. Of the closing words the commentators divide: Clarke cannot tell whether the prophet, the messenger or the king speaks them, and suggests the prophet answering the messenger from within, while Ellicott calls Ewald’s correction certainly right, that the king and not the messenger is meant.
